The code of the A/B testing deck, in the order of the deck. The mobile operator of the churn session tests its retention e-mail in Germany and Spain; the outcome is a click on the link. The data are simulated, one row per customer, and sit two folders up in `data/abtest/`. The same code as a plain Python script: `ab_testing.py`; the in-class exercise, `ab_exercise.qmd`, reuses these steps.

| File | Columns |
|---|---|
| `email_ab.csv`: the A/B test, 40,000 customers | `customer_id`, `country` (DE, ES), `device` (mobile, desktop), `version` (A = generic subject line, B = with the first name), `clicked` (1 = clicked the link), `unsubscribed` (1 = left the mailing list) |
| `email_factorial.csv`: the 2 × 2 test, 40,000 customers | the same columns, with `personal` (1 = first name) and `discount` (1 = 10 % off the next bill) instead of `version` |

```{python}
# the packages of slide 30; Steps 1 to 3 repeat their imports, as on the slides
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from plotnine import (aes, facet_wrap, geom_histogram, geom_hline, geom_line, geom_point, geom_vline,
                      ggplot, labs)
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.anova import anova_lm
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize, proportions_ztest
```

## Step 1: load and check the split

The code of slide 31: customers, clicks and click rate per version, and the test of the counts against the planned 50:50 split (SRM, sample ratio mismatch).

```{python}
import polars as pl
from scipy import stats

ab = pl.read_csv("../../data/abtest/email_ab.csv")

split = (ab.group_by("version")
         .agg(pl.len().alias("n"),
              pl.col("clicked").sum().alias("clicks"),
              pl.col("clicked").mean().alias("click_rate"))
         .sort("version"))
stats.chisquare(split["n"].to_list()).pvalue  # SRM
split
```

A notebook shows only the last line of a chunk, so we print the SRM p here, next to the invented broken split of slide 17.

```{python}
# SRM p of our split and of the broken split of slide 17 (20,000 vs 19,300)
print("SRM p, our test:", round(stats.chisquare(split["n"].to_list()).pvalue, 3))
print("SRM p, broken split:", round(stats.chisquare([20_000, 19_300]).pvalue, 4))
```

Our SRM p is 1.000, so the split is as planned; the broken split gives 0.0004, below 0.001: stop and look for the bug.

```{python}
# balance check: the share on mobile and from Spain per version (slide 10)
(ab.group_by("version")
 .agg((pl.col("device") == "mobile").mean().alias("share_mobile"),
      (pl.col("country") == "ES").mean().alias("share_spain"))
 .sort("version"))
```

The coin flip made the groups alike: 59.5 % vs 59.9 % read on mobile, and 50 % come from Spain in both (10,000 per version and market).

## Step 2: difference, z-test, CI and power

The code of slide 32. Index 0 is version A and index 1 is version B, so the sign is B − A; the last line asks how many customers per version detect 3.3 % → 3.9 % with 80 % power.

```{python}
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import (
    proportions_ztest, confint_proportions_2indep,
    proportion_effectsize)
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower

x, n = split["clicks"].to_list(), split["n"].to_list()
z, p = proportions_ztest([x[1], x[0]], [n[1], n[0]])
lo, hi = confint_proportions_2indep(x[1], n[1],
                                    x[0], n[0])   # B - A

es = proportion_effectsize(0.039, 0.033)
NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)
```

The chunk shows only the sample size: 15,106.9, so 15,107 customers per version. The other results, in percentage points (pp):

```{python}
# B − A in pp, the relative lift, z, p and the 95 % CI
diff = x[1] / n[1] - x[0] / n[0]
print("B - A in pp:", round(diff * 100, 2))
print("relative lift in %:", round(diff / (x[0] / n[0]) * 100, 1))
print("z:", round(z, 2), " p:", round(p, 4))
print("95 % CI in pp:", round(lo * 100, 2), "to", round(hi * 100, 2))
```

B adds 0.60 pp (3.33 % → 3.93 %, +18 % relative); the effect is plausibly between 0.23 and 0.97 pp. The unsubscribe rate is the guardrail, tested the same way:

```{python}
# guardrail: the unsubscribe rate per version and its z-test (slide 15)
unsub = (ab.group_by("version")
         .agg(pl.len().alias("n"),
              pl.col("unsubscribed").sum().alias("unsubscribes"),
              pl.col("unsubscribed").mean().alias("unsub_rate"))
         .sort("version"))
u, nu = unsub["unsubscribes"].to_list(), unsub["n"].to_list()
print("unsubscribes, B - A in pp:", round((u[1] / nu[1] - u[0] / nu[0]) * 100, 3))
print("unsubscribes, p:", round(proportions_ztest([u[1], u[0]], [nu[1], nu[0]])[1], 3))
unsub
```

Unsubscribes rise from 0.31 % to 0.41 % (+0.105 pp, p 0.079): within noise, but watch it in the next send.

## Step 3: the factorial regression and plot

The code of slide 33. `personal * discount` gives the two factors and their product term; OLS on 0/1 clicks is a linear probability model, so the coefficients × 100 are pp.

```{python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from plotnine import aes, geom_line, geom_point, ggplot

fa = pl.read_csv("../../data/abtest/email_factorial.csv")
m = smf.ols("clicked ~ personal * discount",
            data=fa.to_pandas()).fit()
m.params * 100                     # in pp

cells = (fa.group_by("personal", "discount")
         .agg(pl.col("clicked").mean().alias("rate")))
(ggplot(cells, aes("discount", "rate",
                   colour="factor(personal)"))
 + geom_line() + geom_point())
```

The plot was the last line, so here are the coefficients in pp:

```{python}
(m.params * 100).round(2)          # in pp
```

Each coefficient is a cell difference: the intercept is the control cell (3.51 %), `personal` the name without the discount (+0.40), `discount` the discount with the generic subject line (+1.59), and `personal:discount` the interaction (+1.02 pp).

```{python}
# the four cells: customers, click rate and unsubscribe rate, and the SRM check (slide 23)
fa_cells = (fa.group_by("personal", "discount")
            .agg(pl.len().alias("n"),
                 pl.col("clicked").mean().alias("click_rate"),
                 pl.col("unsubscribed").mean().alias("unsub_rate"))
            .sort("personal", "discount"))
print("SRM p:", round(stats.chisquare(fa_cells["n"].to_list()).pvalue, 3))
fa_cells
```

10,000 customers per cell (SRM p 1.000). The first name with the discount has the highest click rate (6.52 %) and the fewest unsubscribes (0.24 %).

## Step 4: chance and power

### A/A tests: what chance looks like

Slides 15 and 17: we send the same e-mail (click rate 3.3 %) to two groups of 20,000, 2,000 times, and keep the gap B − A and whether the z-test says p < 0.05.

```{python}
# 2,000 simulated A/A tests (seed 7)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
gaps, significant = [], []
for run in range(2000):
    y = rng.random(40_000) < 0.033
    a, b = y[:20_000].sum(), y[20_000:].sum()
    gaps.append(100 * (b - a) / 20_000)
    significant.append(proportions_ztest([a, b], [20_000, 20_000])[1] < 0.05)
aa = pl.DataFrame({"gap_pp": gaps, "significant": significant})
```

```{python}
# how often chance alone looks "significant", and how rare our +0.60 pp is
print("share with p < 0.05:", aa["significant"].mean())
print("SD of the gaps in pp:", round(aa["gap_pp"].std(), 3))
print("share with a gap of 0.60 pp or more:", (aa["gap_pp"].abs() >= 0.6).mean())
(ggplot(aa, aes("gap_pp")) + geom_histogram(binwidth=0.05) + geom_vline(xintercept=0.6, colour="blue")
 + labs(x="Difference B − A in 2,000 A/A tests (pp)", y="Number of tests"))
```

About 5 % of the A/A tests come out "significant" (5.9 %), the gaps scatter with an SD of 0.18 pp, and only 0.15 % reach 0.60 pp: our result is not chance.

### Power and sample size

Slide 16: the customers per version for three effect sizes from 3.3 %, with 80 % power at the 5 % level, rounded up.

```{python}
# customers per version for 3.3 % → 3.9 %, 3.6 % and 4.3 %
for p1 in [0.039, 0.036, 0.043]:
    need = NormalIndPower().solve_power(proportion_effectsize(p1, 0.033), alpha=0.05, power=0.8)
    print(p1, np.ceil(need))
```

Half the effect needs about four times the customers (58,072 instead of 15,107). The power curve for +0.6 pp (`es` from Step 2):

```{python}
# power for 1,000 to 40,000 customers per version
n_grid = np.arange(1_000, 40_001, 1_000)
curve = pl.DataFrame({"n": n_grid, "power": NormalIndPower().power(es, nobs1=n_grid, alpha=0.05)})
print(curve.filter(pl.col("n").is_in([2_000, 5_000, 10_000, 20_000, 40_000])))
(ggplot(curve, aes("n", "power")) + geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept=0.8, linetype="dashed")
 + labs(x="Customers per version", y="Power"))
```

With our 20,000 per version the test had 89.7 % power; with 2,000 it would have had only 17.5 %.

## Step 5: does B work for everyone? Device as a moderator

```{python}
# customers, clicks and click rate by device and version (slide 18)
device = (ab.group_by("device", "version")
          .agg(pl.len().alias("n"),
               pl.col("clicked").sum().alias("clicks"),
               pl.col("clicked").mean().alias("click_rate"))
          .sort("device", "version"))
device
```

```{python}
# customers, B − A in pp and the z-test of Step 2 within each device
mob = device.filter(pl.col("device") == "mobile")
desk = device.filter(pl.col("device") == "desktop")
print("customers on mobile and desktop:", mob["n"].sum(), desk["n"].sum())
print("mobile: B - A in pp", round((mob["click_rate"][1] - mob["click_rate"][0]) * 100, 2))
print("desktop: B - A in pp", round((desk["click_rate"][1] - desk["click_rate"][0]) * 100, 2))
print("p mobile:", round(proportions_ztest(mob["clicks"].to_list(), mob["n"].to_list())[1], 4))
print("p desktop:", round(proportions_ztest(desk["clicks"].to_list(), desk["n"].to_list())[1], 4))
```

B adds +0.92 pp on mobile (3.33 % → 4.25 %, p 0.0002) and only +0.13 pp on desktop (p 0.66). Is that difference more than chance? A moderator is tested with a product term:

```{python}
# B × mobile in one regression: does the effect of B depend on the device?
d = ab.with_columns(B=(pl.col("version") == "B").cast(pl.Int64),
                    mobile=(pl.col("device") == "mobile").cast(pl.Int64))
m_device = smf.ols("clicked ~ B * mobile", data=d.to_pandas()).fit()
print("B:mobile in pp:", round(m_device.params["B:mobile"] * 100, 2))
print("p:", round(m_device.pvalues["B:mobile"], 3))
```

B adds 0.79 pp more on mobile (p 0.038). A segment found after the test is a hypothesis: confirm it in a new test.

## Step 6: the 2 × 2 by hand and the two-way ANOVA

### By hand: simple effects, main effects, interaction

Slide 24. A simple effect compares two cells within one level of the other factor, the main effect is the average of the two simple effects, and the interaction is their difference.

```{python}
# the effects from the four click rates of Step 3, in pp
r00, r01, r10, r11 = fa_cells["click_rate"].to_list()   # personal, discount: 00, 01, 10, 11
pl.DataFrame({
    "effect": ["name, no discount", "name, with discount", "discount, generic", "discount, first name",
               "main effect name", "main effect discount", "interaction"],
    "pp": [r10 - r00, r11 - r01, r01 - r00, r11 - r10,
           (r10 - r00 + r11 - r01) / 2, (r01 - r00 + r11 - r10) / 2, (r11 - r01) - (r10 - r00)],
}).with_columns((pl.col("pp") * 100).round(2))
```

The name adds +0.40 pp without and +1.42 pp with the discount; the interaction, +1.02 pp, is the same whichever factor we start from. Report the simple effects: the main effect of the name (+0.91 pp) fits neither e-mail.

### Regression and two-way ANOVA

Slide 25: one model, two read-outs. The regression table gives each cell difference with its p-value; the two-way ANOVA (`typ=2`) tests the two main effects and the interaction.

```{python}
# the model of Step 3: coefficients with p-values, then the two-way ANOVA
print(m.summary())
anova_lm(m, typ=2)
```

The interaction has p 0.017 in both read-outs (t = 2.40, F = 5.75 = 2.40²); F for the main effects is 18.32 (name) and 97.56 (discount).

```{python}
# effect coding (−0.5 / +0.5): the coefficients are the main effects; SEs in pp
fa_e = fa.with_columns(pe=pl.col("personal") - 0.5, de=pl.col("discount") - 0.5)
m_e = smf.ols("clicked ~ pe * de", data=fa_e.to_pandas()).fit()
print((m_e.params * 100).round(2))
(m_e.bse * 100).round(2)
```

With effect coding the main effects are +0.91 pp (name) and +2.10 pp (discount). The SE of the interaction (0.43 pp) is twice that of a main effect (0.21 pp), so an interaction of the same size needs about four times the customers (slide 28).

## Step 7: the logit reads the interaction differently

Slide 26: the same model as a logit. Its coefficients are on the log-odds scale; `np.exp` turns them into odds ratios.

```{python}
# the 2 × 2 as a logit: log-odds coefficients and odds ratios
lg = smf.logit("clicked ~ personal * discount", data=fa.to_pandas()).fit(disp=0)
print(np.exp(lg.params).round(2))   # odds ratios
lg.summary()
```

```{python}
# the four cells on the log-odds scale: log(rate / (1 - rate))
fa_cells.with_columns(log_odds=(pl.col("click_rate") / (1 - pl.col("click_rate"))).log())
```

In log-odds the name adds 0.11 without and 0.26 with the discount, a product term of 0.149 (OR 1.16, p 0.124); in click rates it is +1.02 pp (p 0.017). The discount raises the base rate, so the same odds lift is worth more pp: read interactions in pp, the scale of the decision.

## Step 8: does the interaction differ by market?

```{python}
# the regression of Step 3 in each market: the interaction in pp (slide 27)
germany = fa.filter(pl.col("country") == "DE").to_pandas()
spain = fa.filter(pl.col("country") == "ES").to_pandas()
m_de = smf.ols("clicked ~ personal * discount", data=germany).fit()
m_es = smf.ols("clicked ~ personal * discount", data=spain).fit()
print("Germany:", round(m_de.params["personal:discount"] * 100, 2), "pp, p",
      round(m_de.pvalues["personal:discount"], 3))
print("Spain:", round(m_es.params["personal:discount"] * 100, 2), "pp, p",
      round(m_es.pvalues["personal:discount"], 3))
```

"Significant in Spain, not in Germany" is not a test of a difference. The three-way term tests it directly:

```{python}
# the difference of the interaction, Spain − Germany
m_three = smf.ols("clicked ~ personal * discount * C(country)", data=fa.to_pandas()).fit()
term = "personal:discount:C(country)[T.ES]"
print("Spain - Germany in pp:", round(m_three.params[term] * 100, 2))
print("p:", round(m_three.pvalues[term], 3))
```

The gap of +1.36 pp has p 0.110: within chance. The data were simulated with the same interaction (+1.0 pp) in both markets; still, repeat a test in each market before a roll-out.

```{python}
# click rate per cell and market, one panel per market
markets = (fa.group_by("country", "personal", "discount")
           .agg(pl.col("clicked").mean().alias("rate"))
           .sort("country", "personal", "discount"))
print(markets)
(ggplot(markets, aes("discount", "rate", colour="factor(personal)"))
 + geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_wrap("country")
 + labs(x="Discount", y="Click rate", colour="First name"))
```

## Appendix: open data for practice

Three open datasets for your own A/B lab (slide 39); none is downloaded here.

- **Hillstrom MineThatData E-Mail Analytics Challenge (2008):** 64,000 customers of a US retailer, randomised to a men's e-mail, a women's e-mail or no e-mail; free CSV from minethatdata.com, no licence stated.
- **Upworthy Research Archive** (Matias et al. 2021, Scientific Data): 4,873 headline tests of a news site, randomised within each test; CC BY 4.0, <https://osf.io/jd64p>.
- **Criteo Uplift Prediction Dataset v2.1:** online ads, random treatment and control, about 14 million rows; CC BY-NC-SA, non-commercial use only.
